items.title: Catch me if you can: Inside flash demonstrations by student groups against Gyanesh Kumar
items.summary: At the Delhi protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the police seemed to have a clear plan: get to the protesters before they could raise their slogans. But the protesters had a plan of their own: make sure the police had to keep running. Between October 11 and 13, the capital’s streets saw many flash demonstrations, with student activists darting across Connaught Place, Janpath and other parts of the city, appearing suddenly and disappearing into police detention within minutes. Flags emerged from pockets, groups materialised from different directions, and even a tea break in Connaught Place came with an unexpected protest. These demonstrations followed a crackdown on mobilisation. With activists alleging that restrictions made it increasingly difficult to protest, student groups turned to decentralised mobilisation, last-minute announcements and small groups to make their voices heard. Newslaundry reporters ran alongside protesters across the capital to understand how these demonstrations were organised, how word spread, and how activists attempted to dissent despite restrictions. The spectacle left commuters and shopkeepers baffled. Amid the commotion, security personnel attempted to detain a man who had started running alongside the crowd. The man kept running until restaurant staff intervened to explain that he was one of their employees. The security personnel then let him go. For a few moments, it was difficult to tell who was protesting, who was trying to avoid detention and who had simply been swept up in the commotion. People interested in participating in protests often communicated directly with one another and made their way to Connaught Place independently,” he said. Detained on Sunday evening, I saw three policemen pummel almost everyone who boarded after me: two stood at the van’s door at the back, and the third inside the corridor, which opened into mesh-covered, cage-like enclosures. Once each citizen entered the corridor, they were hit in the abdomen, elbowed hard in the back, kicked and worse. One youngster was pushed to the floor and beaten there. Another was viciously stamped on. These assaults were systematic, seemed to last roughly similar lengths of time for each person being detained, and served as the prologue to the shove into the cages. Earlier that evening, at around 4 pm, while sloganeering against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, a small group of student protesters from Disha Student Union (Disha Chhatra Sangathan) was intercepted by Delhi Police at the junction of Panchkuian Road and Outer Circle at Connaught Place in central Delhi. Thereafter, while photographing the ensuing mayhem as Delhi Police bundled protesters into DTC buses and a convict van, I was picked up as well. Cops were stationed at its mouth on Outer Circle. Once inside, it was impossible to escape. Once off the bus, men and women were separated. We were told to sit on the road where some protesters were already squatting . The women were taken deeper into the corral, and I lost sight of them. Our group would swell further. items.title: Delhi High Court rules it can execute commercial decrees below ₹2 crore if original suit was within its jurisdiction
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has held that it can execute a decree arising from a commercial suit even if the amount sought to be recovered is below its ₹2 crore pecuniary jurisdiction threshold, provided the original suit was within its jurisdiction [Ozone SPA Vs Co-incept] Justice Subramonium Prasad held that a court does not lose its jurisdiction to execute a decree merely because the decretal amount falls below its pecuniary threshold. " The contention that alteration in pecuniary limit of the court which passed the decree would also take away the power of such Court to execute the said decree cannot be accepted ," the Court observed. Justice Subramonium Prasad The ruling came in an execution petition filed by Ozone Spa Private Limited against Co-Incept Hospitality Private Limited and others, seeking enforcement of a ₹1.19 crore decree passed in July 2018. The dispute arose from a franchise agreement executed in December 2013, under which Co-Incept Hospitality was permitted to operate a gym, spa and salon under the Ozone brand at Rajouri Garden in Delhi. Following disputes over royalty payments, Ozone Spa filed a commercial suit seeking recovery of ₹2.53 crore and a permanent injunction. The parties subsequently entered into a settlement agreement in July 2018, based on which the High Court passed a consent decree. Ozone Spa later alleged that the judgment debtors breached the settlement by failing to issue post-dated cheques, defaulting on royalty payments and closing the outlet without notice. One of the judgment debtors challenged the maintainability of the execution petition, arguing that the ₹1.19 crore sought to be recovered was below the ₹2 crore threshold applicable to the High Court's Commercial Division. The High Court rejected the objection. It relied on Sections 37 and 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), which permit a decree to be executed by the court that passed it or by another court to which it is transferred. The Court also referred to earlier Delhi High Court decisions holding that changes in pecuniary jurisdiction do not automatically deprive a court of its power to execute decrees already passed by it. The Court further clarified that Sections 37 and 38 of the CPC apply to decrees passed under the Commercial Courts Act. items.title: Only 45 stations closed, no complete metro ban: DMRC to Supreme Court; Chairperson tenders apology
items.summary: The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has told the Supreme Court that there was no complete ban on metro services on the day of the proposed protests at Jantar Mantar. It said that only 45 of its 303 stations were closed for entry and exit on October 10, after the Supreme Court on October 9 ordered that there shall be no outright prohibition on the movement of metro trains. DMRC Chairperson D Thara has also tendered an "unconditional apology" in an affidavit filed in response to a contempt notice issued on October 11. On October 9, a Bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant took up an oral mentioning against Delhi Police communications. These had asked DMRC to shut entry and exit gates at 57 stations and reduce train frequency. The Court said that the notifications appeared "overreaching, as they impose a complete ban upon essential public transportation." The Bench had clarified there "shall be no outright prohibition on the movement of Metro trains". It said that any regulated arrangement should be "widely publicised". DMRC, the Railways and Delhi Police (Traffic) were directed to file compliance reports within four days. In a special Sunday hearing on October 11, the Court was informed that metro stations were still closed despite its orders. It thus said that a prima facie case of contempt of court has been made out over the alleged violation of its October 9 direction. In her affidavit, Thara said the order had been complied with "in letter and spirit". She said that the matter was taken up ex-parte, as DMRC had neither been served nor appeared. The police notification, she said, "did not impose a complete ban on public transportation. It merely directed the closure of 57 out of the 303 stations for entry and exit purposes." After the Court's order, the police cut the list to 45 stations, dropping 12, the affidavit said. DMRC claimed there was "zero reduction in the total volume of metro operation". It said that 271 trains ran 4,157 trips on the standard Saturday schedule. According to DMRC, 14 interchange stations, including Rajiv Chowk, Kashmere Gate and Central Secretariat, continued to allow passengers to change lines. Exit gates stayed open at Vishwavidyalaya, it said, and Gate No. 3 was kept open at GTB Nagar. items.title: NCLAT stays insolvency proceedings against Polycab India over ₹2.78 crore debt
items.summary: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) has stayed insolvency proceedings against cable and wire manufacturer Polycab India Limited over an alleged operational debt of ₹2.78 crore. [Bharat Ajay Jaisinghani v. Asier Metals Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.] NCLAT's principal bench comprising officiating chairperson Justice Yogesh Khanna and technical members Barun Mitra and Ajai Das Mehrotra granted interim relief on October 9 in an appeal filed by Bharat Ajay Jaisinghani, the suspended director of Polycab. The tribunal directed that the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) be kept in abeyance, subject to Polycab depositing the entire claimed amount of ₹2.78 crores. Senior Advocate Arun Kathpalia , appearing for Jaisinghani, submitted that Polycab was ready to deposit the sum without prejudice to its rights and contentions. Kathpalia pointed to pre-existing disputes over credit notes and highlighted Polycab's standing as India's largest integrated cable manufacturer. The NCLAT bench observed in its order: “Though the existence of dispute has been agitated by the Respondent (Asier) but suffice is to say that considering the status of the Appellant (Polycab) as above as also the fact the Appellant is inclined to deposit an amount, though without prejudice to its rights and contentions, let the said amount be deposited and that the impugned order is stayed and be kept in abeyance till further orders,” the NCLAT recorded in its order. The appeal challenged an October 7 order of the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitting a Section 9 IBC plea by operational creditor Asier Metals Private Limited over aluminium ingot supplies. Polycab had opposed the insolvency arguing that invoices reflected ‘provisional billing’, ledgers required reconciliation and an ₹80 lakh deduction for demurrage was pending. The NCLT bench of judicial member Shammi Khan and technical member Sanjeev Sharma rejected Polycab's defence. “Item on the Purchase Order states that the purchase price for products payable by Polycab shall be as specified in the PO, fixed, firm, and cannot be varied without the prior written consent from Polycab... items.title: Indian Youth Congress head moves Delhi High Court against Jantar Mantar's de-notification as protest venue
items.summary: Indian Youth Congress (IYC) President Uday Bhanu Chib has approached the Delhi High Court, challenging the denotification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest venue. An earlier plea filed by Chib challenging provisions of the Delhi Police' standing order on protests is already pending before the High Court. He has moved an application in the same plea, challenging the police's order of October 11 de-notifying Jantar Mantar as the designated protest spot. The standing order said that Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground, and CBD Ground, East Delhi, have been designated as new protest venues in place of Jantar Mantar. According to the order, the decision was taken in line with the recommendations of a committee constituted by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs to examine alternate venues for citizens' protests and demonstrations. " Based on the Committee's recommendations, Jantar Mantar as a protest venue has been de-notified. Three new venues viz Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground, East Delhi have been designated as new venues for organizing protest/demonstrations ," the order said. The order comes amid protests against the Election Commission of India and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and massive police crackdowns on the same in the national capital. The Delhi Police justified this decision before the High Court on Tuesday, stating that the decision was taken based on an order passed by the Supreme Court on October 9. A separate plea challenging the standing order is pending before the Supreme Court.

items.title: Personality Rights vs Freedom of Expression - Finding a balance
items.summary: John Stuart Mill The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it. Freedom of speech and expression has long been regarded as a cornerstone of constitutional democracy. In India, it is guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India, 1950, and embodies the liberty to communicate ideas, share information, and engage in creative expression. Yet, freedom of speech and expression has never been understood to be absolute. During the Constituent Assembly debates, members grappled with the limits of fundamental rights and recognised the need to reconcile individual liberty with competing interests. The significance of this debate continues to hold relevance even today, particularly when the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression overlaps and traverses with other fundamental rights. In continuation of this debate, in recent years, the Courts in India have repeatedly been called upon to address the growing conflict between personality rights, recognised under the broader framework of Article 21, and the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Personality rights, often used interchangeably with ‘celebrity rights’ or ‘publicity rights’, broadly concern an individual’s ability “ to control commercial use of human identity ” . These rights protect unique attributes such as an individual’s name, image, voice, likeness, and other distinctive characteristics against unauthorised appropriation and commercial exploitation. In R Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu , when personality rights were considered for the first time, the Supreme Court held that the unauthorised use of a person’s name or identity constitutes an invasion of privacy. The law has since evolved to recognise publicity rights as protecting the commercial value associated with an individual’s persona , with its enforcement requiring proof of identification and commercial exploitation. Later decisions , however, extended and expanded the scope of protection without requiring proof of falsity, confusion, or deception. items.title: Lawyer moves Supreme Court challenging de-notification of Jantar Mantar as protest site
items.summary: A petition has been filed before the Supreme Court challenging the Delhi police order dated October 11 by which Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a designated protest site in Delhi and three alternative venues were notified in its place. The matter is likely to be listed for hearing tomorrow. Delhi Police de-notified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest venue. Instead, Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground, East Delhi have been designated as new venues for holding protests. A standing order to this effect was issued by Delhi Commissioner of Police Anurag Kumar dated October 11. According to the order, the decision was taken in line with the recommendations of a committee constituted by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs to examine alternate venues for citizens' protests and demonstrations. The Delhi Police also justified this decision before the High Court in a case filed by the Indian Youth Congress. In that case, the police said that the decision was taken based on the Supreme Court's order of October 9. The petition before the Supreme Court, filed by advocate Swaty Singh, contends that the move violates the fundamental rights to freedom of speech and expression and to assemble peacefully under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution. While the State can regulate these rights in the interest of public order, the petition states that such regulation cannot operate as a prohibition or render the exercise of these rights illusory. It further argues that the location of a protest site is central to the protests. "The right to protest is not merely a right to assemble at a designated physical space; it is a right to communicate grievances, express dissent and draw the attention of the public authorities and society at large towards matters requiring redressal," the petition states. According to the plea, proximity to the concerned institutions, accessibility to the public and visibility to the intended audience directly affect a protest's effectiveness. As per the plea, "Relocating protests to distant or outlying areas of Delhi, particularly where such relocation materially increases the burden of participation and distances demonstrators from the authorities to whom their grievances are addressed, may substantially diminish the communicative purpose of peaceful assembly." items.title: You ate his ear off, how do we replace it? Supreme Court to man seeking bail in assault case
items.summary: "You ate his ear, how do we replace it?" the Supreme Court asked a man on Wednesday, giving short shrift to his petition for anticipatory bail in an assault case. Injecting a dose of dry judicial wit into the hearing, a Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran made it clear that a litigant accused of chomping off a neighbour's ear during a street clash could hardly expect pre-arrest protection. The matter reached the top court on an appeal challenging a February 2026 order of the Jharkhand High Court, which had refused anticipatory bail to one Rajiv Ranjan Kumar over a violent clash in Ranchi. Kumar's counsel attempted to soften the blow by painting the incident as a routine neighbourhood feud that simply spiralled out of control on a festive night. "It’s a long-simmering dispute between neighbours. It flared up on one night and cross-FIRs were registered. The opposite side managed to get anticipatory bail while I was denied the same. The way it started was, it was the night of Janmashtami, people were celebrating and there was some stone pelting..." the counsel submitted. However, the Bench refused to be distracted by the festive backdrop, zeroing in instead on the the injury involved. "Aapne pehle bandook nikali, phir uska kaan pakad liya, aur pura kaan khaa gaye aap. (You first took out a pistol, then held his ear and ate it) And you want anticipatory bail? " the Court remarked. When the counsel protested that the allegation regarding the firearm was fabricated, the Bench offered a swift concession - only to press harder on the remaining damage. "Chalo pistol jaane dijiye. Kaan ka kya karein? (Okay, let the pistol be, what do we do about the ear?) How do we replace it?" the Court quipped. The counsel claimed his client was actually the primary victim of the tussle. "I was pinned down on the ground. My hands and legs were restrained. My chest was bitten..." counsel submitted. "So you admit that there was a brawl?" the Bench interjected. "Yes. I am willing to cooperate with the investigation," the counsel replied. The Bench was not persuaded by the defence of mutual combat and dismissed the petition. The petitioner had been booked under several provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) - including Section 118 (voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means) - following an FIR registered at Argora police station in 2024. items.title: Satyaki Savarkar alleges Rahul Gandhi’s cross-examination amounting to surveillance, prolonging trial
items.summary: Satyaki Savarkar, the grandnephew of VD Savarkar, has filed an objection pursis before the Special MP/MLA Court in Pune, alleging that Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s defence team is conducting a "roving and fishing inquiry" during cross-examination to prolong the defamation trial. [Satyaki Savarkar v. Rahul Gandhi] In the pursis filed on October 14, Savarkar submitted that his cross-examination has spanned an "unreasonable span of more than ten (10) months" without any definitive timeframe provided by the defence. He contended that persistent questions regarding his daily routine, publishing business and attendance at public and cultural events infringe upon his fundamental rights, creating an apprehension of being followed. “Inquiring into Complainant's movements and public presence creates an oppressive atmosphere of surveillance, directly impeding upon his personal liberty and right to privacy,” the pursis stated. Savarkar pointed out that he has scrupulously restricted his case to the facts in issue and "never sought to delve into the Accused's personal movements, foreign visits or private engagements." He urged the court to curb irrelevant inquiries, arguing that the defence is dragging in unrelated political and cultural organisations "merely to politicize the trial and consume the precious judicial time," warning that proceedings "would go on for ages and will be unending." This is the second time Savarkar has sought judicial intervention to regulate the proceedings. On July 30, he filed an application seeking a strict timeline and tighter control over the cross-examination. Judicial Magistrate First Class Amol Shinde issued notice on August 4 seeking Gandhi’s reply, which remains pending. The criminal defamation complaint stems from remarks made by Gandhi during a gathering in the United Kingdom in March 2023. Gandhi allegedly claimed that Savarkar wrote in his memoirs about an incident where he and others assaulted a Muslim man and derived pleasure from the act. Satyaki Savarkar initiated criminal defamation proceedings under Section 500 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and sought compensation under Section 357 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), asserting that no such incident exists in VD Savarkar's published works and accusing Gandhi of distorting history. The hearing will continue on October 28. Advocate Sangram Kolhatkar appeared for Satyaki Savarkar. Advocate Milind Pawar appeared for Rahul Gandhi.

items.title: J&K High Court stays CAT Jammu order imposing ₹10,000 costs on senior advocate
items.summary: The High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh has stayed the operation of an order passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), Jammu Bench, imposing costs of ₹10,000 on Senior Advocate Jahangir Ganai. A Division Bench of Justices Sanjeev Kumar and MA Chowdhary passed the interim order while hearing the senior advocate’s writ petition against the Tribunal’s order. Justice Sanjeev Kumar and Justice M A Choudhary The CAT had imposed the costs after recording that Ganai appeared before it during virtual proceedings without wearing uniform and made derogatory remarks against it. The Tribunal had also observed that he appeared to be unapologetic about appearing without uniform. After hearing counsel for the parties, the High Court observed that “the case for indulgence at this stage is made out.” The Division Bench expressed its intention to mediate and explore an amicable settlement. The Court directed the tribunal members concerned and the petitioners to appear in person before it in chambers on October 21. “In the meanwhile, there shall be stay of the effect and operation of the impugned order,” the High Court directed. Senior Advocate UK Jalali , along with Advocates Prachi Sharma, KS Johal, Supreet Singh Johal, Pranav Kohli, Rounak Gupta, Aseem Kumar Sawhney, A.K. Sawhney, Aman Sharma, M Shabab Malik, Harish Singh, Anil Kumar, Simran Shale, Madeeha Latief and Kamil Nazir appeared for Ganai. Senior Advocate Abhinav Sharma , assisted by Advocate Abhirash Sharma, appeared for respondent Mohd Amin Dar and others. Additional Advocate General Rajesh Thappa and Advocate Pawan Kundal appeared for the State. [Read order]

items.title: Won't accept lame excuses, produce it: Supreme Court slams ECI for claiming it lost 2023 Karnataka vote-counting video
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday pulled up the Election Commission of India (ECI) for claiming that it was unable to trace the 2023 video recording of the counting of votes in Karnataka's Sringeri assembly constituency. The Court was hearing a case related to the election dispute between Congress leader TD Rajegowda and BJP candidate DN Jeevaraj. Rajegowda had won the assembly elections from Sringeri assembly constituency in 2023 by a narrow margin of 201 votes. However, the Congress candidate was recently unseated after a recount declared that Jeevaraj had secured more votes. In May, the top court granted Rajegowda relief by directing that he shall remain the Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA) during the pendency of his plea. Today, a bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva expressed surprise after the ECI said that it was unable to trace the video recording of the counting that took place in 2023. "How can the Election Commission of India (ECI) say that it has lost its record? Your whole purpose is to hold an election, and you need to have a document. Where is the question of you saying, ‘Yeah, we are trying to trace it’? You gave it to the elected candidate. There is no custody of records. Whatever you have, produce it on the next date. Otherwise, we will have to draw an adverse inference against you. We will not accept these kinds of lame excuses," the Court said. We will not accept these kinds of lame excuses. The Court noted that the Congress MLA wants to see the observer's report and video recordings of the original vote counting and the recent recounting. When the Court said it will direct the ECI to produce these documents and video recordings, Senior Advocate Seshadri Naidu for the ECI said it was unable to trace the video of 2023. items.summary: Trinamool Congress (TMC) leader Mahua Moitra on Wednesday disputed a claim made by the State government before the Calcutta High Court that she has been provided "X" level security as per her entitlement as a Member of Parliament (MP) [ Mahua Moitra v. State of West Bengal ]. The submission was made before Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya during the hearing of Moitra's plea for upgraded security following the Tehatta egg-pelting incident in Nadia. The Court proceeded to grant Moitra time place her submission (about the current status of her security cover) on record by filing a supplementary affidavit. The matter will be heard next on December 2. Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya During an October 7 hearing of the matter , the Court had asked the State if there were any guidelines on the security cover or protection to be given to dignitaries like MPs. At the time, Moitra's counsel had submitted that there is a "Yellow Book" which contains guidelines on how MPs should be given protection, which was a highly confidential document in the State's custody. Today, the State's Additional Advocate General (AAG) Rajdeep Mazumder told the Court that Moitra, being an MP, is entitled to "X" category protection under the norms laid down in the Ministry of Home Affairs' Yellow Book. This includes one Personal Security Officer (PSO) equipped with side arms who would accompany the MP round the clock. He further said that one such PSO was already provided to Moitra. The Court went on to observe that if Moitra wanted to be granted more protection, she would have to show why such security upgradation is required. "If yellow book says that she is ‘X’ protectee, you (Moitra) have to demonstrate that you are entitled to get more security or enhanced or upgraded security ... in order to get an order, as you have prayed for in this writ petition, you are required to demonstrate to this Court that under the relevant procedure, you are entitled to get upgradation of security cover," Justice Bhattacharya said. items.title: J&K High Court says doctors hesitant to perform abortions without court order, aggrieved mothers left at God's mercy
items.summary: The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court recently observed that doctors refuse to perform abortions even in cases where the procedure is legally permitted under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act. Justice Mohd Yousuf Wani made the comment while dealing with a case of a woman who, despite serious foetal abnormalities, had to approach the Court for medical termination of pregnancy after doctors refused to perform abortion without judicial order. The Court emphasised that medical practitioners should not unnecessarily avoid attending emergent cases for which statutory directions under the MTP Act and relevant rules are clear. "The registered medical practitioners especially doctors working in the associated hospitals of medical colleges and in other district hospitals do not shoulder their statutory responsibilities in terms of the provisions of Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 and the rules of 2003 framed thereunder in justified cases thereby leaving the aggrieved mothers at the mercy of the God who, in search of some solace feel constrained to shoulder further mental agony and burden of approaching the courts of law for legal directions," the Court said. Justice Mohammad Yousuf Wani Under the MTP Act, termination of pregnancy is permitted up to 24 weeks subject to prescribed conditions, while terminations beyond 24 weeks are highly restricted. The Court further said that clause 2-B of Section 3 and clause 1 of Section 5 of the MTP Act clearly reveal that the provisions relating to length of pregnancy do not apply to termination of pregnancy in cases with substantial foetal abnormalities or where abortion is necessary to save the life of the pregnant women. The order was passed on a petition moved by a couple for directions to constitute a medical board for termination of pregnancy in view of detection of serious abnormalities in the foetus at the gestational age of 31 weeks. On September 29, the doctors told the couple that due to the advanced stage of the foetus, the termination cannot be undertaken without the intervention of the High Court. The couple then moved the Court seeking consideration under the statutory framework governing termination beyond the ordinary gestational limit in cases of substantial foetal abnormalities. items.title: Adani Green Energy moves Karnataka High Court against 1% property tax on solar power plants
items.summary: Adani Green Energy (UP) Limited (petitioner) has approached the Karnataka High Court challenging the State government's amended rules imposing property tax at the rate of 1 percent of the property's value on solar power plants. The company has challenged the Karnataka Grama Swaraj and Panchayat Raj (Grama Panchayat Taxes, Rates and Fees) Rules, 2025, notified on October 17, 2025 to the extent they classify solar power plants as regular industrial buildings for taxation purposes. The petitioner has submitted that it installed a solar power plant within the Bengaluru South districts Channapattana and Magadi Taluku, MB Halli, H Byadarahalli and Mattikere Gram Panchayats and had been paying taxes in accordance with the earlier regime. However, the State government subsequently proposed increasing the tax on renewable energy units from ₹5,000 to ₹10,000 per megawatt. The company has alleged that the final notification issued on October 17, 2025, departed from the earlier proposal and instead brought solar power plants under the category of regular industries, subjecting them to property tax at the rate of 1 percent of the property's value under Schedule I. The same was done without giving any explanation and without calling for objection from all the stakeholders much less from the renewable energy stakeholders, it has been contended. items.title: Delhi SIR: Plea in Supreme Court challenges ECI directive requiring deleted voters to enrol afresh
items.summary: An application has been filed before the Supreme Court challenging the Election Commission of India's (ECI) requirement that voters excluded from Delhi's draft electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) must declare themselves as first-time applicants to secure restoration of their names. The application has been moved by RTI activist Anjali Bhardwaj and another petitioner in their pending petition against the Election Commission. They have sought directions to provide a separate mechanism for restoring the names of previously enrolled voters. The petitioners have pointed out that 47,56,722 electors, constituting 32.78% of Delhi's electorate before the SIR, were excluded from the draft electoral rolls published on August 31. Of these, 31,59,213 were classified as permanently shifted. According to the application, these voters must submit Form 6 to seek re-inclusion, although the form requires applicants to declare that they are seeking enrolment for the first time. The petitioners argue that this places previously enrolled voters in an untenable position, particularly because Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 makes knowingly false declarations punishable with imprisonment extending to one year, a fine, or both. "An elector whose name was previously included in the electoral roll cannot, therefore, reasonably be required to make a declaration that he/she is seeking enrolment for the first time as a pre-condition to seeking restoration of his/her name," the application states. The petitioners have also challenged the additional declaration prescribed under the SIR instructions, arguing that it imposes substantive requirements beyond statutory Form 6 without following the procedure prescribed under Section 28 of the Act. They contend that the additional declaration was neither notified in the official gazette nor placed before the parliament. The application further highlights that between August 31 and October 4, only 569 Form 6 applications were disposed of, compared with 3,209 Form 7 applications concerning objections to inclusion or deletion. items.title: Gauhati High Court grants bail to accused in Zubeen Garg murder case
items.summary: The Gauhati High Court recently granted bail to Amritprava Mahanta, an accused in the alleged murder of Assamese singer Zubeen Garg, after finding that the investigation materials and evidence recorded during trial did not disclose a prima facie case against her [Amritprava Mahanta v. State of Assam]. Justice Pranjal Das observed that continuing Mahanta's detention despite the absence of supporting evidence would amount to a travesty of justice. " Considering the nature of the materials found on record so far, with regard to A-4 Amritprava Mahanta, it would be a travesty of justice to deny her bail at this stage, especially when she has already undergone undertrial detention for almost a year now, " the Court said. Justice Pranjal Das Garg died in Singapore on September 19, 2025, after an incident during a yacht trip. Following complaints alleging murder, the Assam Police's Criminal Investigation Department registered a case and eventually chargesheeted seven persons. Mahanta was accused of participating in a conspiracy to murder Garg by supplying him alcohol despite knowing about his medical condition, including epilepsy and seizures. However, the Court found that none of the 250 witnesses examined during investigation stated that Mahanta served, administered or forced alcohol upon Garg. It further noted that the testimonies of 124 prosecution witnesses examined during trial did not substantiate the allegation. The Court also found no material indicating that Mahanta had organised Garg's Singapore visit, arranged the yacht trip or encouraged him to swim without a life jacket. " The prima facie case of A4 being involved in conspiracy to murder the victim is not made out from the investigation materials and trial testimony so fa r," the Court observed. Justice Das also emphasised that courts must decide cases according to the evidence rather than public sentiment. Court said, " A court has to be conscious of society’s sense of justice, but cannot be captive to it ." Taking into account Mahanta's nearly year-long incarceration, lack of criminal antecedents and statutory provisions concerning bail for women, the Court granted her bail on a bond of ₹50,000 with two sureties. She was directed to cooperate with the trial, refrain from influencing witnesses and not travel abroad without permission. The Court clarified that its observations were confined to the bail proceedings and would not affect the ongoing trial. Senior Advocate AK Bhuyan , assisted by Advocat

items.title: Justice Indira Banerjee explains why fewer women are appointed as arbitrators
items.summary: Former Supreme Court judge Justice Indira Banerjee recently explained that the relatively low number of women appointed as arbitrators is partly attributable to the historically limited representation of women in the higher judiciary, particularly the Supreme Court. Justice Banerjee was speaking at the launch of Arbitrator Appointments in Numbers , an empirical study prepared by the Milon K. Banerji Arbitration Centre (MKBAC) at NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad. The Centre is chaired by former Supreme Court Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman , with Senior Advocate Ritin Rai serving as Co-Chair and Advocate Dr. Amit George as Director (Research). Senior Advocate Gourab Banerji is its Donor and Patron, while Advocates Shreya Parikh and Chand Chopra serve as Associate Directors (Research). The research team comprised Adishree Krishnan, Aditi Bhojnagarwala, Arnav Mathur, Hamza Khan, Mahika Roy, Manav Pamnani and Zorawar Almeida. The report was technically edited by Hruthika Addlagatta and Sukaina Naqvi, while Eluckiaa Asaithambi served as Faculty Coordinator. The discussion also featured Delhi High Court judge Justice Prateek Jalan, Bombay High Court judge Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan , Senior Advocates Gourab Banerji and Ritin Rai, along with researchers from the Centre who presented the report's findings. items.title: Plea in Supreme Court seeks contempt action against Congress party for post against CJI
items.summary: A petition filed before the Supreme Court has sought guidelines to bar political parties from running public campaigns that target a judge or the Chief Justice of India (CJI) in relation to pending matters, outside the procedure for removal of judges laid down in the Constitution. The plea has been filed following a post by the X handle of the Kerala unit of the Congress on October 12, which said, "Dear Surya Kant, If law and order is not your domain, resign now. We will find your replacement who can handle it." The petition says the post addressed the CJI by name, without the courtesy of his title and sought to coerce a sitting Chief Justice who had declined to discuss sub-judice matters outside the courtroom. It also refers to a post by Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra the same evening, "Surya clearly Can't. So we will." Besides the Union government, the Congress Party, Rahul Gandhi, Mallikarjun Kharge, Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee, Mahua Moitra and Akhilesh Yadav have been made respondents to the plea. The plea says that Articles 121 and 124(4) provide the exclusive mechanism for removing a judge, and the demand by the Congress Kerala Unit was an attempt to overawe the Chief Justice which the constitutional scheme forbids. The petition also says that the claim that a party would find the CJI's replacement is contrary to the constitutional scheme for appointing judges. It has also cited the resolutions of the Supreme Court Bar Association and the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association condemning the calls for the CJI's resignation. The petition has sought directions to initiate criminal contempt proceedings against the respondents after giving them notice and a hearing. The plea has been filed by advocates Digant Mishra, Divyansh Bisht, Ashish Gopal Garg and Shweta Garg through Advocate-on-Record Utkarsh Jaiswal. A Division Bench of Justice Devan Ramachandran and Justice Basant Balaji observed that although the adverse remarks were meant to caution young lawyers about their professional duties, such remarks could permanently affect the lawyer's legal career. items.title: Emerald Heights International School moves Supreme Court seeking curbs on children's social media use
items.summary: Emerald Heights International School and its Director Siddharth Singh have moved the Supreme Court seeking restrictions on children's use of social media and an enforceable regulatory framework to protect them from online harms. The petition contends that protecting children from environments detrimental to their health, dignity and development is a constitutional responsibility of the State, and cannot be left solely to parental supervision or corporate goodwill. It has sought a direction to the Central government to frame, notify and operationalise a dedicated, comprehensive and enforceable regulatory framework to protect children on social media platforms. Alternatively, the plea seeks a prohibition on social media use by children below a prescribed age and regulation of use above that age, or enforceable age-based restrictions on children's accounts on designated platforms. The plea has invoked Article 39(f) of the Constitution, which directs the State to ensure that children develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity. The plea has also cited Article 39(e), concerning protection against abuse of children's tender age. It also relies on Article 21, the State's public health obligations under Article 47 and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. The petition flags a range of harms linked to social media use, including depression, anxiety, compulsive use, social comparison, body-image dissatisfaction, disordered eating, sleep disruption and cyberbullying. It also points to grooming, sexual exploitation, coercion involving intimate images, exposure to violent, sexually explicit, self-harm and suicide-related content, as well as behavioural profiling and compulsive-use design. According to the petitioners, such harms may develop unnoticed until serious damage has occurred, and cannot be adequately addressed through reassuring statements, voluntary platform measures or parental controls alone. The petition seeks a declaration that the continuing failure to protect children against these foreseeable risks is arbitrary and violative of Articles fundamental rights including right to equality and right to life. The petition was filed through advocate Vaibhav Choudhary and drawn by advocates Khusbhu Jain, Mayank Singh Rawat and Zaid Ahmed. items.title: First come first serve policy to allot grounds for Ramleela unfair: Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has directed Delhi government authorities to frame comprehensive guidelines every year for allotment of public grounds for Ramleela and similar cultural or religious events [Ray of New Beginning Foundation v. Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board & Ors] . Justice Amit Mahajan passed the order on October 8, holding that a “first come, first serve” policy for allotment of such spaces is constitutionally unreasonable and can create unequal opportunities for applicants. The Court reasoned that at first sight, the expression “first come first serve” seems to embody an objective rule, but it creates an unequal race for information by incentivising the discovery of availability of a public ground before competing applicants become aware of it. “The same creates a structural dilemma, that is, a person with privileged access to administrative information may obtain an advantage that is unavailable to others,” the Court said. Justice Amit Mahajan, Delhi High Court Therefore, it directed the authorities to publish annual site-allocation notices at least 90 days before the first scheduled event. The Court said that notices must specify available grounds, application timelines, eligibility conditions, evaluation criteria and grievance-redressal mechanisms. Where multiple eligible applicants compete for a site, authorities must conduct a comparative assessment using a predetermined, published scoring matrix or other published criteria, the Court said. It clarified that previous organisers may receive limited preference based on their compliance record but cannot enjoy an automatic right to allotment. Such preference should not extend beyond two consecutive years where competing eligible applicants exist. “The annual timetable must be designed so that the final allotment and ordinary grievance process are completed sufficiently before the event begins,” the Court ordered. The Bench passed the order while hearing a plea filed by Rays of New Beginning Foundation challenging the rejection of its application to organise Ramleela at a ground in Delhi. items.title: Strict NDPS Act bail conditions not a must if recovered drug only marginally above commercial quantity: Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently observed that when the drugs recovered from an accused are only marginally above the commercial quantity threshold, the stringent bail conditions under Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act (NDPS Act) need not be applied in their full rigour [Sunny v State of NCT of Delhi] Justice Amit Bansal made the observation while hearing a bail plea of a man arrested in July 2025 after alleged recovery of 259.3 grams of morphine. The commercial quantity for morphine is 250 grams. "In such circumstances, the strict application of the rigours of the NDPS Act may not be justified and warrants a more nuanced consideration," the Court said. Justice Amit Bansal According to the prosecution, the accused Sunny was caught during regular police patrolling. His disclosure led the police to a co-accused, from whom 114 grams of morphine was recovered. The co-accused was granted bail by a Sessions Court in May this year. The counsel for Sunny argued that he had been falsely implicated and that no independent public witness was joined during the search despite people being present at the spot. He added that charges had been framed but no witness has been examined so far. The State opposed the plea, contending that Section 37 was attracted and that the accused could not claim parity since the co-accused was found with an intermediate quantity. It also pointed to a previous FIR against him. Relying on a series of Supreme Court rulings, the Court said the Section 37 requirements do not preclude grant of bail on the grounds of undue delay in the completion of the trial. It added that the evidence was yet to begin and "will take considerable time." The Court thus granted bail to the accused. Advocates Shan Ul Islam, S Islam and Dinesh Chandar appeared for the accused. Additional Public Prosecutor Mukesh Kumar appeared for the State, along with Sub-Inspector Arvind Kumar of the Crime Branch. items.title: Madras HC upholds turncoat AIADMK MLAs’ resignations, sets 2-month deadline for disqualification pleas
items.summary: The Madras High Court on Tuesday upheld the Tamil Nadu Assembly Speaker’s decision to accept the resignations of six MLAs who switched allegiance to the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) party soon after they were elected on an AIADMK ticket [ Agri Krishnamurthy v. Speaker ]. A Bench of Chief Justice SA Dharmadhikari and Justice Arul Murugan , however, also held that acceptance of the resignations did not render disqualification proceedings pending against the MLAs academic or infructuous. The Speaker must still adjudicate those proceedings, and his determination would carry the consequences prescribed under the Tenth Schedule (concerning political defection) of the Constitution, the Court said. The Court, therefore, directed the Speaker to decide the pending disqualification proceedings against the former AIADMK MLAs within two months. CJ SA Dharmadhikari and Justice Arul Murugan The Court passed the verdict on a plea filed by AIADMK leader and party Whip Agri Krishnamurthy. He challenged the decision of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly Speaker to accept the resignation of six AIADMK MLAs, S Jayakumar, Maragatham Kumaravel, P Sathyabama, Esakki Subbaya, C Vijaya Bhaskar and MR Vijayabhaskar. The six MLAs resigned after defying the AIADMK Whip and voting in favour of the Chief Minister Joseph Vijay-led TVK government during a confidence motion. The MLAs were inducted into TVK soon after the vote, and their resignations were accepted by the Speaker the same day. In his plea, Krishnamurthy argued that the Speaker could not have accepted their resignations when disqualification proceedings against them were pending. The plea argued that the Speaker ought to have conducted a meaningful inquiry before accepting the resignations, particularly since allegations of horse-trading and inducement had already been raised. Krishnamurthy also challenged gazette notifications declaring the Assembly seats from where the resigned MLAs contested vacant. The plea stated that under Article 190 of the Constitution, an MLA’s resignation does not automatically result in a vacancy. The Speaker must first satisfy himself that the resignation is voluntary and genuine, the Court was told. The Court today dismissed his plea. It held that resignation and disqualification are distinct constitutional processes, and the pendency of disqualification proceedings did not prevent the Speaker from accepting the resignations. The Speaker was represented by Advocate General Vijay Narayan Senior

items.title: Old Monk sale ban has cost Maharashtra ₹350 crore in revenue: Company tells Bombay High Court

FSSAI claimed that incorporating artificial or nature-identical rum flavoring masks a spirit's natural compositions. FSSAI’ decided to halt Old Monk sales over the labels as well as misleading ageing descriptors, such as '7 years old blended' and 'very old vatted'. The High Court had earlier declined an immediate interim stay on the prohibition. items.summary: The Karnataka High Court on Monday struck down the provisions of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and of Appointments or Posts in the Services under the State) Act, 2022, which increased reservation for Scheduled Castes (SCs) from 15 to 17 percent and for Scheduled Tribes (STs) from 3 to 7 percent [Mahendra Kumar Mitra & others Vs Union of India & others]. A bench of Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice K S Hemalekha held that Section 3 of the Act, insofar as it took the aggregate reservation beyond the 50 percent ceiling, violated Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution. The Court also struck down Section 4, which provided for the enhanced reservation in State government services. Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice KS Hemalekha The Court passed the decision on two petitions challenging the constitutional validity of the legislation, which increased the overall reservation for SCs, STs and other backward classes from 50 to 56 percent. “Section 3 of the Act, insofar as it takes the aggregate reservation beyond the ceiling of 50%, is struck down as it violates Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution,” the Court held. One of the petitions was filed by Mahendra Kumar Mitra, State President of the Dr Ambedkar Scheduled Castes Federation. Another Petition was filed by Sagar H R, Prajwal Kumar D and Purushotham Gowda G M, graduates in civil engineering who had applied for appointment to the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) in the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP). The petitioners challenged the increase in reservation in State government appointments, contending that the legislation breached the constitutional limit on reservation and affected the guarantee of equality and equal opportunity. The Act, which received the Governor's assent on January 11, 2023, was published in the Karnataka Gazette on January 12, 2023, and was deemed to have come into force from November 1, 2022. Under Section 3, reservation for SCs and STs in admissions to educational institutions was increased to 17 percent and 7 percent, respectively. Section 4 increased their reservation in State government services from 15 to 17 percent and from 3 to 7 percent, respectively. Since the 32 percent reservation for other backward classes remained unchanged, the overall reservation rose from 50 to 56 percent. items.title: Madras HC questions Tamil Nadu police over repeated denial of RSS route marches
items.summary: The Madras High Court on Wednesday, October 14, questioned why Tamil Nadu police repeatedly denied the RSS permission for route marches despite earlier court directions. Justice V Lakshminarayanan asked why the organisation could hold marches in Jammu and Kashmir but faced repeated restrictions in Tamil Nadu. “If they (RSS) can have a march in a terrorist infested place like Jammu and Kashmir, why is the Tamil Nadu police denying permission to them every year?” the court asked, according to LiveLaw. The report said that the judge also criticised the state government for denying permission for processions organised by both the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Dravidar Kazhagam (DK), forcing them to approach the court. “This government is against any procession. They're denying permission for Dravidar Kazhagam and for RSS,” the court remarked. It also said the government appeared to be treating citizens as enemies by refusing permission for protests. “The government is seeing citizens as enemies. Whichever government is coming up, they're rejecting,” the judge said. The remarks came during the hearing of a petition filed by RSS member VG Jagadeesan, who sought permission for route marches on October 18, October 25, November 1, or other dates. The proposed marches would feature members in uniform, accompanied by a musical band, followed by public meetings. Senior advocate NL Rajah, appearing for Jagadeesan, told the court that the RSS was repeatedly denied permission and had to approach the judiciary every year. He said the organisation wanted to conduct the march to mark its foundation day, which coincides with Vijayadashami, but police rejected its applications citing possible law and order problems. Rajah also questioned the impact of the repeated denials on smaller organisations that could not afford to approach the court. “An organisation like the RSS is able to come to court and seek permission. But what about the smaller parties which do not have the wherewithal to come to court?” he asked. Advocate General Vijaya Narayan, appearing for the state, told the court that permission had been denied because the proposed public meetings were to be held at locations not designated for such gatherings. The court directed five representatives of the petitioners to meet State Public Prosecutor John Sathyan to discuss arrangements for conducting the marches peacefully. items.title: Journalist as witness to State brutality: A story from Delhi’s Pandwalan Khurd
items.summary: Delhi Police is beating protesters after detaining them. I saw this firsthand while sitting inside the blue, mesh-windowed van the police usually uses to ferry prisoners and undertrials between prisons and courts. Detained on Sunday evening (October 11), I saw three policemen pummel almost everyone who boarded after me: two stood at the van’s door at the back, and the third inside the corridor, which opened into mesh-covered, cage-like enclosures. Once each citizen entered the corridor, they were hit in the abdomen, elbowed hard in the back, kicked and worse. One youngster was pushed to the floor and beaten there. Another was viciously stamped on. These assaults were systematic, seemed to last roughly similar lengths of time for each person being detained, and served as the prologue to the shove into the cages. Earlier that evening, at around 4 pm, while sloganeering against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, a small group of student protesters from Disha Student's Organisation (Disha Chhatra Sangathan) was intercepted by Delhi Police at the junction of Panchkuian Road and Outer Circle at Connaught Place in central Delhi. Thereafter, while photographing the ensuing mayhem as Delhi Police bundled protesters into DTC buses and a convict van, I was picked up as well. What follows is an eyewitness account of what happened. The corral at Regal Cinema We were first taken to Regal Cinema, where Delhi Police had used barricades to corral off half the width of Sansad Marg, along a stretch that seemed to run the length of Regal Building. Cops were stationed at its mouth on Outer Circle. Once inside, it was impossible to escape. Once off the bus, men and women were separated. We were told to sit on the road where some protesters were already squatting . The women were taken deeper into the corral, and I lost sight of them. Our group would swell further. items.title: Thousands of votes marked for deletion in Andhra Pradesh without reasons on record
items.summary: In just the last 12 days of the claims and objections period, 40,006 names were filed under form 7 as part of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision in Andhra Pradesh. Of these, 20,959 (52.38%) name election officials as objectors. The consolidated statements also do not contain the reason for asking for deletion. Form 7 is the application form used by the Election Commission of India to object to the inclusion of a name or to request the deletion of an existing name from the electoral rolls. Since the start of the claims and objections period under the SIR, the ECI has been publishing a consolidated statement of the total number of Form 7 applications received on a given day on its website . This consolidated statement, called Form 10, contains the name of the objector, the person whose name they are objecting to, polling station details and the reason for objection. TNM analysed data between 29 September and October 10 – the last date for filing claims and objections in Andhra Pradesh. We were unable to access Form 10 uploaded prior to 29 September as Form 10s are available online only for a week. The claims and objections period for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Andhra Pradesh lasted from July 31 to October 10 – a total of 72 days. We found that in the constituencies with the highest deletions, the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) or the (Assistant Electoral Registration Officer) was named as the objector. Applicants submitting Form 7 are required to select one of the five justifications mentioned in the form. The reasons are the person is dead, underage, absent/permanently shifted, already enrolled or not an Indian citizen. We noticed that when Form 7s are filed by normal citizens, the consolidated statement carries the reason for objection. But the reason for objection is not listed when an ERO or AERO is the objector. In the top 20 constituencies with the highest deletions, the ERO/AERO was listed as the objector on Form 7 in 16,241 cases out of 21,115 cases. This accounts for 76.91% of cases in 20 constituencies alone.
